cmo-cjmo-2024-01.title: Count responses; give a construction
cmo-cjmo-2024-01.body:
**Two detectors are not enough.** Each detector answers yes or no, so two detectors produce at most $2 \times 2 = 4$ different response patterns, but there are $8$ possible cells. Two cells would give the same responses.

**Three detectors suffice.** Use detector $1$ = the whole first row $[1,1] \times [1,4]$, detector $2$ = the first two columns $[1,2] \times [1,2]$, detector $3$ = the middle two columns $[1,2] \times [2,3]$. The detectors containing each cell are:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline 1,2 & 1,2,3 & 1,3 & 1 \\ \hline 2 & 2,3 & 3 & \text{none} \\ \hline\end{array}$$
All eight cells give different response patterns, so the responses determine the cell.

**Answer: $Q = 3$.**

cmo-cjmo-2024-02.title: Group by the maximum
cmo-cjmo-2024-02.body:
Since $\min\left\{\frac1i, \frac1j, \frac1k\right\} = \frac{1}{\max(i, j, k)}$, group the $n^3$ triples by $\ell = \max(i,j,k) \in \{1, \dots, n\}$. The number of triples with all entries at most $\ell$ is $\ell^3$, and with all entries at most $\ell - 1$ is $(\ell-1)^3$; so exactly
$$\ell^3 - (\ell - 1)^3 = 3\ell^2 - 3\ell + 1$$
triples have maximum $\ell$. Hence
$$I_n = \sum_{\ell=1}^n \frac{3\ell^2 - 3\ell + 1}{\ell} = \sum_{\ell=1}^n \left(3\ell - 3 + \frac1\ell\right) = \frac{3n(n+1)}{2} - 3n + H_n.$$
Therefore
$$I_n - H_n = \frac{3n(n+1)}{2} - 3n = \frac{3n(n-1)}{2}.$$
(Check: $n = 1$ gives $I_1 = 1 = H_1$; $n = 2$ gives $I_2 = 1 + 7\cdot\frac12 = \frac92$ and $H_2 = \frac32$, difference $3$.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{3n(n-1)}{2}$.**

cmo-cjmo-2024-03.title: Reflect $A$ onto $BC$
cmo-cjmo-2024-03.body:
Let $\ell_1$ be the reflection of line $AB$ in $CI$ and $\ell_2$ the reflection of line $AC$ in $BI$. We use directed angles between lines, modulo $180^\circ$; a reflection reverses directed angles.

**Points on $BC$.** The line $CI$ bisects angle $ACB$, so the reflection in $CI$ swaps the lines $CA$ and $CB$. Hence the reflection $F$ of $A$ in $CI$ lies on line $CB$, and $F \in \ell_1$. Since $I$ lies on the mirror, $IF = IA$. Similarly the reflection $E$ of $A$ in $BI$ lies on line $BC$ and on $\ell_2$, and $IE = IA$. So $IE = IF$.

Moreover $E \ne F$: $F$ is on ray $CB$ with $CF = CA = b$, and $E$ is on ray $BC$ with $BE = BA = c$. A common point of the two rays lies on segment $BC$, and $E = F$ would give $b + c = a$, contradicting the triangle inequality.

**$XE = XF$.** The reflection in $CI$ maps line $CB$ to line $CA$ and $\ell_1$ to line $AB$, so
$$\measuredangle(BC, \ell_1) = -\measuredangle(CA, AB).$$
The reflection in $BI$ maps line $BC$ to line $BA$ and $\ell_2$ to line $AC$, so
$$\measuredangle(BC, \ell_2) = -\measuredangle(AB, AC).$$
Since $-\measuredangle(CA, AB) = \measuredangle(AB, AC)$, this says $\measuredangle(BC, \ell_1) = \measuredangle(AB, AC) = -\measuredangle(BC, \ell_2)$.
Let $s$ be the line perpendicular to $BC$ through the midpoint of $EF$, and $\sigma$ the reflection in $s$. Then $\sigma$ maps $BC$ to itself, swaps $E$ and $F$, and reverses directed angles with $BC$; so $\sigma(\ell_1)$ is the line through $E$ making directed angle $-\measuredangle(BC, \ell_1) = \measuredangle(BC, \ell_2)$ with $BC$, i.e. $\sigma(\ell_1) = \ell_2$ and likewise $\sigma(\ell_2) = \ell_1$. Since $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ meet in the single point $X$, $\sigma(X) = X$, so $X \in s$.

**Conclusion.** $I$ is also on $s$ because $IE = IF$. Finally $X \ne I$: as $I$ lies on the mirror $CI$, $I \in \ell_1$ would mean $I \in AB$, which is false since $I$ is inside the triangle. Therefore the line $XI$ is $s$, which is perpendicular to $BC$. ∎

cmo-cjmo-2024-04.title: The product would be a perfect square
cmo-cjmo-2024-04.body:
**No.** Each of the $2024$ numbers appears in exactly two adjacent pairs, so the product of all $2024$ adjacent products equals the square of the product of the numbers. Thus $P = 1! \cdot 2! \cdots 2024!$ would have to be a perfect square.

Group the factorials in pairs: $(2i-1)!\,(2i)! = \bigl((2i-1)!\bigr)^2 \cdot 2i$. Hence
$$P = \prod_{i=1}^{1012}\bigl((2i-1)!\bigr)^2 \cdot \prod_{i=1}^{1012} 2i = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{1012}(2i-1)!\right)^2 \cdot 2^{1012} \cdot 1012!,$$
and $2^{1012} = (2^{506})^2$. So $P$ is a perfect square if and only if $1012!$ is. But $1009$ is prime and $1009 \le 1012 < 2 \cdot 1009$, so $1009$ divides $1012!$ exactly once; hence $1012!$ is not a perfect square, and neither is $P$.

So Jane cannot do it. **Answer: No.**

cmo-cjmo-2024-04.title: A prime between $506$ and $1012$
cmo-cjmo-2024-04.body: As before, $P = 1! \cdot 2! \cdots 2024!$ would have to be a perfect square. Take the prime $p = 1009$. Since $p^2 > 2024$, $v_p(j!) = \lfloor j/p \rfloor$ for $j \le 2024$: it is $0$ for $j < 1009$, $1$ for $1009 \le j \le 2017$ ($1009$ values) and $2$ for $2018 \le j \le 2024$ ($7$ values). So $v_{1009}(P) = 1009 + 2 \cdot 7 = 1023$, which is odd. So $P$ is not a perfect square and the answer is **No**.

cmo-cjmo-2024-05.title: Reverse the digits
cmo-cjmo-2024-05.body:
Let $f(x) = d_9x^9 + \dots + d_1x + d_0$.

**$d_0 = 0$.** Then $f(x) = x \cdot (d_9x^8 + \dots + d_1)$ with the second factor of degree $8$, so $f$ is reducible. So every irreducible $f$ has $d_0 \ne 0$.

**Reversal.** For a polynomial $p(x) = a_n x^n + \dots + a_0$ of degree $n$ with $a_n a_0 \ne 0$, define $\bar p(x) = a_0x^n + a_1x^{n-1} + \dots + a_n = x^n p(1/x)$. It again has degree $n$ and nonzero constant term, and $\bar{\bar p} = p$. If $d_0 \ne 0$, then $\bar f$ corresponds to the reversed digit string $\overline{d_0d_1\cdots d_9}$, again a $10$-digit number (leading digit $d_0 > 0$, constant term $d_9 > 0$).

**Reversal preserves reducibility.** Suppose $f = gh$ with $\deg g, \deg h \ge 1$ (rational coefficients). The leading and constant coefficients of $f$ are products of those of $g$ and $h$, so all are nonzero, and $\deg \bar g = \deg g$, $\deg \bar h = \deg h$, $\deg g + \deg h = 9$. Then
$$\bar f(x) = x^9 f(1/x) = x^{\deg g} g(1/x) \cdot x^{\deg h} h(1/x) = \bar g(x)\,\bar h(x),$$
a factorization of $\bar f$ into non-constant factors. Applying this to $\bar f$ (whose reversal is $f$) gives the converse. So $f$ is irreducible iff $\bar f$ is.

**Palindromes are reducible.** If $\bar f = f$, then $d_i = d_{9-i}$ for all $i$. Since $i$ and $9 - i$ have opposite parities,
$$f(-1) = \sum_{i=0}^{9} (-1)^i d_i = \sum_{i=0}^{4} \bigl((-1)^i d_i + (-1)^{9-i} d_{9-i}\bigr) = \sum_{i=0}^{4} (-1)^i (d_i - d_{9-i}) = 0,$$
so $(x + 1) \mid f$, and $f$ (of degree $9$) is reducible.

**Conclusion.** The irreducible polynomials in question all have $d_0 \ne 0$ and $\bar f \ne f$, and the involution $f \mapsto \bar f$ maps irreducible ones to irreducible ones without fixed points. So they split into pairs $\{f, \bar f\}$, and $N$ is even. ∎
